Trump and Xi Could Learn Something From Darwin

Survival depends on adaptation. For the United States and China, that may include cooperation.

By Fareed Zakaria, the host of CNN’s Fareed Zakaria GPS and the author, most recently, of Age of Revolutions.

FP’s analysis and reporting

By now, the world has heard about the Hugging Face attack in July, in which OpenAI agents broke into Hugging Face, a leading American AI platform. What is less well known is how this attack ended. Hugging Face said it tried to use AI to analyze the incident and respond. But the typical American frontier models refused to help because their safety guardrails couldn’t distinguish between investigating a cyberattack and carrying one out.
So Hugging Face turned to a Chinese model: GLM-5.2, developed by China’s Z.ai, which helped investigators understand the attack.
To summarize: An American AI broke into an American technology company. To figure out what happened, the company ended up using a Chinese AI.
Or consider what has happened with the price of oil. The United States has waged a war with Iran, one of the world’s leading oil producers. Experts predicted that the price of oil would skyrocket even higher if the war lasted several months, many suggesting it would hit $150 a barrel. But that hasn’t happened. Why? The single biggest cause is probably that China, for its own reasons, chose to reduce its imports of oil by a staggering 4 million barrels a day, approximately. If not for that Chinese action, gas prices in the U.S. would be far higher than they are today.
In his excellent new book “Darwin’s Lock,” Joshua Cooper Ramo points out that when developing his theory of evolution, Charles Darwin struggled to explain phenomena like altruism or self-sacrifice using purely competitive, zero-sum logic. He came to realize that in a merciless environment, species often “lock” into cooperative arrangements not as acts of kindness but because mutual support is the only viable path to fitness.
Something like that characterizes the U.S.-China relationship. These two countries have spent four decades growing within the same economic and technological ecosystem. Supply chains, capital, research, manufacturing and markets became intertwined. This is true not just for the U.S. but for most countries worldwide, all of which have deep ties with China.
In Washington (and in parts of Beijing) people talk about a new Cold War between America and China. But the analogy is misplaced. America and the Soviet Union were largely unconnected—economically, technologically, culturally. But China and the U.S. are deeply intertwined, and these ties can be severed only at great cost to both sides—and the global economy.
Take pharmaceuticals. The nonprofit United States Pharmacopeia finds that roughly 41 percent of the key starting materials used in U.S.-approved medicines are sole-sourced from China. According to Brookings, that dependence is particularly high for antibiotics and the inputs used for statins, antidepressants and blood-pressure medications. FDA data show that as of last year, of the manufacturers that supplied the U.S. market with the key ingredients in any medicine, only about 9 percent were domestic, compared with 22 percent in China and 44 percent in India. So we are all dependent.

Trump Can’t Force a Global Decoupling From China

If the goal of his trade war is a coalition against Beijing, it will backfire in three ways.

Analysis
|

Agathe Demarais

We tend to hear “survival of the fittest” and imagine nature as an endless struggle in which one creature devours another. But evolutionary fitness actually means the ability to adapt successfully to changing conditions. Nature is full not just of competition but of specialization, symbiosis and cooperation.
Ramo applies that insight to international affairs. He does not imagine America and China becoming friends. He expects fierce technological competition, military rivalry and political distrust. But he argues that the two countries have evolved inside the same system to such a degree that attempts by one to weaken the other increasingly ricochet back on the other. His stark alternatives are “coevolution” or “coextinction.”
There is an obvious objection. Interdependence can be weaponized. The U.S. should worry when China has near-monopolies over materials essential to American industry. China also worries about depending on American technology for the chips powering its AI revolution. But reducing a set of dependencies in a few areas is very different from a broader decoupling of the world’s two largest economies.
A better term than “weaponized interdependence” might be “managed interdependence.” It gives up on two fantasies at once: the old idea that more trade automatically produces peace, and the new idea that national security requires severing every connection with a rival.
Instead, map the connections. Where dependence creates an unacceptable vulnerability, diversify and build alternatives. Where economic ties benefit both sides without creating serious security risks, don’t destroy them simply to prove toughness. And where the two countries remain deeply connected, build firebreaks so that a conflict in one area doesn’t cascade throughout the entire relationship.
For 30 years, we made one mistake about globalization: We assumed trade would eradicate geopolitics. Now we risk making the opposite mistake—assuming geopolitics can simply erase the realities of a global, deeply interconnected economy.
